statements: The chief concern is a slowly enlarging right cheek mass in a 4-year-old boy.
The right cheek mass has been present for 1 year.
The right cheek mass is notably asymptomatic.
The key clinical task is to determine the most likely cause of a pediatric buccal soft-tissue mass based on its growth pattern, exam characteristics, and imaging.
The lesion is 3 × 2 × 1 cm.
The lesion is firm.
The lesion is non-tender.
The lesion is non-fluctuant.
The lesion is non-pulsatile.
The lesion is freely mobile between the buccal mucosa and skin.
The lesion has distinct margins.
The overlying mucosa is normal.
The lesion extends from the right oral commissure to the pterygomandibular raphe.
The lesion suggests a buccal space or intramuscular location.
Aspiration yielded no fluid.
Ultrasound confirmed a soft-tissue mass.
Contrast CT showed a well-defined hypodense lesion within the muscle layer.
CBC was normal.
The metabolic panel was normal.
There was no submandibular lymphadenopathy.
There was no submental lymphadenopathy.
There is no pain.
There is no tenderness.
There is no dysphagia.
There is no dysphonia.
There is no dyspnea.
There is no trauma.
There are no systemic symptoms.
There is no lymphadenopathy.
There is no mucosal discoloration.
There is no pulsatility.
There is no fluctuance.
There was no aspirated fluid.
These findings make inflammatory or infectious causes less likely.
These findings make aggressive malignant lesions less likely.
These findings make many vascular lesions less likely.
Intramuscular lipoma fits well with a slowly enlarging, painless, well-circumscribed, mobile soft-tissue mass.
CT showing a well-defined hypodense lesion within the muscle layer strongly supports a fatty lesion.
The intramuscular location matches an intramuscular lipoma.
Lack of lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms also supports a benign mesenchymal tumor.
Dermoid and epidermoid cysts can present as painless, slow-growing cheek masses in children.
Aspiration yielded no fluid.
The lesion was described as firm rather than doughy or cystic.
CT localization within the muscle layer is less typical for a dermoid or epidermoid cyst.
Pediatric cheek masses commonly include vascular lesions.
The lesion was non-pulsatile.
The lesion was non-fluctuant.
The mucosal color was normal.
Aspiration yielded no blood or fluid.
CT described a well-defined hypodense intramuscular lesion without vascular features.
A painless intramuscular mass could raise the possibility of rhabdomyoma or another benign mesenchymal tumor.
Rhabdomyoma and other benign mesenchymal tumors are much rarer than lipoma.
CT density described as hypodense is more characteristic of fat.
Malignancy such as rhabdomyosarcoma is less likely because the lesion has been slowly enlarging over a year.
Malignancy such as rhabdomyosarcoma is less likely because the lesion is well defined.
Malignancy such as rhabdomyosarcoma is less likely because the lesion is freely mobile.
Malignancy such as rhabdomyosarcoma is less likely because the lesion is painless.
Malignancy such as rhabdomyosarcoma is less likely because there is no lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms.
Imaging does not suggest an infiltrative aggressive mass.

The combination of a long-standing painless cheek mass, benign exam features, absence of inflammatory or malignant signs, and a well-defined hypodense lesion within the muscle layer on CT most strongly indicates a lipomatous tumor arising in muscle.
The most likely diagnosis is intramuscular lipoma of the cheek or buccinator region.
Intramuscular lipoma is the high-probability differential diagnosis.
Dermoid or epidermoid cyst is a medium-probability differential diagnosis.
Vascular malformation or hemangioma is a low-probability differential diagnosis.
Rhabdomyosarcoma or other malignant soft-tissue tumor is a low-probability differential diagnosis.
The final diagnosis is intramuscular lipoma.
